El-Sayed Takes the Lead in Michigan Senate Race, Cook Report Says 🏆

Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has emerged as the new favorite in Michigan’s closely watched U.S. Senate race, according to an updated assessment by the Cook Political Report. The shift signals growing momentum for Democrats in a contest that could play a significant role in determining control of the Senate.

Cook Political Report has moved the race from its previous “Toss-up” rating to “Lean Democrat,” indicating that El-Sayed now has an advantage over Republican candidate Mike Rogers. The revised outlook comes amid a changing political landscape and new signs of support consolidating behind the Democratic contender.

The assessment is particularly notable given the recent political developments surrounding Haley Stevens, who previously competed against El-Sayed in the Democratic primary but has since backed Rogers. Her decision was seen as an unexpected development that could complicate efforts to unite Democratic voters behind their nominee.However, recent polling suggests that El-Sayed has maintained a strong position. 

A New York Times/Siena College survey reportedly showed him leading Rogers by 11 percentage points, reinforcing the view that the Democratic candidate has gained ground in the race. Jessica Taylor, a Cook Political Report analyst, pointed to the latest polling trends as evidence that Democratic voters are increasingly rallying around El-Sayed. 

The shift in the rating reflects a broader reassessment of the candidates’ relative positions as the election approaches. Michigan is considered a strategically important battleground, and the Senate contest has attracted considerable attention from both parties. A Democratic victory could strengthen the party’s position in the upper chamber, while a Republican win would provide an important opportunity for the GOP to expand its influence in Washington.

Although the new rating gives El-Sayed an advantage, it does not guarantee victory. The final outcome will depend on turnout, voter preferences and the candidates’ ability to maintain momentum through the closing stages of the campaign. For Democrats, the updated forecast offers an encouraging sign in a race that had previously been considered too close to call.

The Alliance Gets an Invoice

Abdul El-Sayed wants Washington to stop treating “ally” as a blank check.

Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee told CBS’s 60 Minutes that U.S. policy promises Palestinians a state while arming people working to prevent one. He accused Israel of genocide in Gaza and called for a fundamental reassessment of the relationship. Israel denies the charge, and the International Court of Justice has not yet ruled on the merits of the genocide case.

His objection extends beyond Israel. He said American tax dollars should fund schools, roads and health care rather than weapons for Israel, Egypt, Saudi Arabia or Pakistan.

He framed his test for an alliance as a parable about a bear. If your companion insists on provoking the animal, El-Sayed argued, you should reconsider the friendship. 

The metaphor leaves something out: Washington has its own decision-makers. President Trump took the United States to war with Iran, and whatever pressure Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu applied does not erase presidential responsibility.

El-Sayed also blamed political spending for insulating the alliance from scrutiny, citing AIPAC’s effort to defeat him in the Democratic primary. That spending is part of his case, but it does not show that every supporter of Israel has been bought.

The questions he puts before voters are legitimate. What does America receive, what does it finance and where should support end? Calling a country an ally does not settle them, and neither does calling it a bad friend.

🖥 Iran says its position on Palestinian self-determination unchanged since 1947

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iran’s principled position on the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination has remained unchanged since 1947, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said on Tuesday.

“If violations of the right to self-determination, the usurpation of land and genocide are considered permissible in the international system, no rule or norm in the world will remain sustainable,” Baqaei said at a national conference on the Palestinian issue.
​
Rejecting attempts to portray Iran’s position as purely ideological, he said Tehran’s support for Palestine stemmed from its civilizational identity and longstanding opposition to oppression and injustice.
​
He stressed that Palestinians must be allowed to exercise their right to self-determination without foreign interference, adding that all governments were legally obligated to support the realization of this fundamental right.
​
Baqaei said countries defending Palestinian rights were fulfilling their binding obligations under international law, while those acting against them were committing clear violations of human rights and international principles.
​
He also criticized international inaction over the continuing genocide in Palestinian territories, saying efforts by international judicial bodies to hold Israeli regime officials accountable were facing obstruction and passivity.
​
The spokesperson stressed that the Palestinian issue went beyond political calculations and was fundamentally a humanitarian matter, adding that the displacement of people, aggression and genocide could not be accepted by the Iranian nation.
